summary: Examines the location privacy problem in Mobile IPv6, where the addresses in signaling or data packets can reveal where a mobile node is and how it moves. It proposes solutions to hide that information. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If your mail always shows the address of where you are, anyone can follow you around. This document looks at ways to keep a roaming device's whereabouts private.

questions: how to protect location privacy in mobile ipv6
does mobile ipv6 reveal a node's location
what is a pseudo home address
how does encrypted home address work
subtitle: Two solutions to hide a roaming device's real address and location from eavesdroppers.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 allows devices to roam while staying reachable, but IP addresses in signaling and data packets reveal the device's real home address and current location to eavesdroppers and even to other parties communicating with the device.
tldr.mechanism: Two solutions are proposed: one encrypts the home address while keeping the device's real address with the peer (for existing sessions), and another uses a randomly generated pseudo home address to hide the real address from peers and eavesdroppers alike (for new sessions).
tldr.outcome: Mobile IPv6 devices can protect their location privacy by choosing an approach appropriate to their situation. Both solutions work with standard Mobile IPv6 procedures and IPsec.

today: RFC 5726 is Experimental and represents the consensus of the IRTF Mobile IP research group. It provides practical techniques for location privacy in Mobile IPv6, though widespread deployment depends on support in both home agents and mobile node implementations.

sections.title: Location Privacy in Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) lets a roaming device remain reachable at a home address on its home network, even when it is attached to a foreign network via a care-of address. The device registers its binding between these two addresses with a home agent on the home network.

The location privacy problem arises because these addresses appear in plaintext in signaling messages (binding updates) and sometimes in data packets. An eavesdropper can see the home address and care-of address together and deduce the device's location and movement patterns. Additionally, a correspondent node (the device the roaming node is communicating with) may see information that reveals the device's real home address.

RFC 5726 proposes two complementary solutions: one protects privacy from eavesdroppers while continuing to use the real home address with peers, and another uses a pseudonym address to hide the real address from both eavesdroppers and peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Your home address is like your real name, and your care-of address is like your current location. When you move, people can see both and track you. These solutions hide one or both so you can roam in secret.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The solutions must follow Mobile IPv6 architecture and must not interfere with IPsec operation or the security association policy between the mobile node and home agent (which is keyed on the real home address). They should provide backward compatibility so that old and new implementations can coexist. The overhead in terms of additional messages or memory should be minimal.

The document assumes that eavesdroppers are passive (they listen but do not modify traffic), that IPsec secures signaling between the mobile node and home agent, and that the home agent is a fixed node. The focus is on location privacy when the mobile node roams to a foreign link; privacy issues when on the home link are outside scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution must work with existing Mobile IPv6, not break security, and not add too much extra stuff sent over the network.

sections.title: The Reverse-Tunneled Solution
sections.content:
The first solution protects location privacy while the mobile node maintains an existing session with a correspondent node using the real home address. During return routability (a standard Mobile IPv6 procedure), the mobile node derives a privacy management key and uses it to encrypt the home address, creating an encrypted home address.

The mobile node then reverse-tunnels a binding update message to the correspondent node via the home agent. Instead of disclosing the real home address directly, the binding update includes the encrypted home address in a new destination option. The correspondent node stores the encrypted home address and uses it in subsequent packets instead of the real address.

The result is that packets sent directly between the mobile node and correspondent node carry only the encrypted home address, which looks different to eavesdroppers for each correspondent node (because the encryption key depends on the correspondent's identity). The home agent and correspondent node can decrypt it, but eavesdroppers cannot derive the real address.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the other person to call you by a secret nickname that you generate especially for them. Everyone else listening only hears the nickname and has no idea where you are.

sections.title: The Pseudo Home Address Solution
sections.content:
The second solution is for cases where the mobile node wants to hide its real home address from the correspondent node itself (typically when initiating a new session). The mobile node generates a pseudo home address by concatenating the home network prefix with a random bit string. This pseudo address is routable (so the home agent can intercept packets sent to it) but is not publicly known.

The mobile node registers the pseudo home address with its home agent during home binding update. In subsequent return routability procedures and binding updates, the mobile node uses the pseudo home address instead of the real address. The correspondent node never learns the real address; it only knows the pseudo one.

Different pseudo home addresses can be used with different correspondent nodes, further preventing correlation of the mobile node's activities. The encrypted home address technique from the first solution can also be applied to the pseudo address for additional protection against profiling attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: You give yourself a random fake address on the home network that is routable but not the real one. You use it with strangers, and they never learn who you really are.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions
sections.content:
Two new mobility options are defined: the Pseudo Home Address option (in home binding updates) and the Pseudo Home Address Acknowledgement option (in binding acknowledgements from the home agent). These allow the mobile node to request pseudo addresses and the home agent to accept or suggest different ones.

Two new IPv6 extension headers are defined: the Encrypted Home Address destination option (for packets sent by the mobile node) and the Encrypted Home Address routing header (for packets received by the mobile node). These carry the encrypted home address or pseudo home address in route-optimized payloads.

A mobile node can detect whether the home agent and correspondent node support these extensions by checking for the appropriate options or headers in responses. If support is not present, the mobile node can choose to proceed without privacy protection, use a different home agent, or abort.
sections.plainLanguage: New labels and tags are added to messages to signal which devices support the privacy solution and to carry the hidden addresses.

sections.title: Threats and Limitations
sections.content:
The solutions protect against passive eavesdropping but assume the home agent and correspondent nodes are trusted. They do not prevent profiling attacks where an attacker correlates multiple flows from the mobile node based on other information (such as the timing of messages, IPsec SPI values, or regular intervals of signaling). The document provides detailed analysis of these profiling vectors in the appendix.

The encrypted home address is keyed on material derived during return routability, which changes when the care-of address changes or the keygen token expires. The pseudo home address is valid only if registered with the home agent and must be within the home network prefix. If the home agent fails or changes, previously used pseudo addresses may no longer be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: These solutions work against someone just watching traffic, but a clever attacker might be able to connect different flows by spotting patterns. The home agent must be trusted, and the addresses stop working if things change.
